name: Individual false lashes / magnetic lashes
lead: False eyelashes are artificial lashes attached to or near the natural lash line to add length, volume or density. Common forms are strip lashes, individual lash extensions applied one at a time by a technician, and magnetic lashes that clamp onto the natural lashes without glue.[1]

Artificial lashes date back more than a century: a 1902-1903 British patent by Karl Nessler and a 1911 US patent by Anna Taylor are recorded, and magnetic lashes were invented in 2014 by Katy Stoka as a glue-free alternative.[1] No clinical studies of individual or magnetic lashes were found.

paras: Strip lashes are synthetic, trimmable strips fixed above the natural lashes with temporary glue and removed with warm water or eye makeup remover.[1] Individual extensions are attached one by one to natural lashes with semi-permanent adhesive, usually by a technician over up to two hours, and last about three to four weeks.[1] Magnetic lashes use a magnetic strip that sandwiches the natural lashes, so no adhesive is needed, and they are reusable.[1]

A report from 1882 described Parisians sewing hair into the eyelids, and a 1899 newspaper account described a similar method as painful. Karl Nessler patented artificial lashes in the UK in 1902-1903, Anna Taylor patented a fabric-strip design in the US in 1911, and false lashes became popular in the early 1930s and again in the 1960s.[1] Magnetic lashes followed in 2014.[1]

Wikipedia notes that magnetic lashes may pose a hazard in MRI scanning rooms because of their magnets, and recounts that an actress's eyes swelled nearly shut after lashes were glued on for a 1916 film.[1] The page does not describe adhesive reactions in detail. A general review of contact dermatitis to cosmetics covers allergic reactions to cosmetic ingredients, though it does not address lashes specifically.[2]
No studies found. Related laboratory work on lash cosmetics includes a 2020 formulation study of a curling mascara using a thermoresponsive polymer, which is not a study of false lashes.[3]

timeline.event: Karl Nessler patents artificial eyelashes in the UK.[1]
Anna Taylor patents false eyelashes in the US.[1]
Doll-like double-lash looks popularised by Twiggy.[1]

card.summary: Glue-on or magnet-on artificial lashes for instant length and volume; the look is temporary and no clinical research exists.
card.note: Magnets may be a hazard in MRI rooms; adhesives can cause reactions.

quick.overview:
Individual false lashes are applied one by one by a technician and last a few weeks, while magnetic lashes clip on with small magnets and are removed daily. Both add apparent length and density.

No clinical studies of either were found.
quick.mechanism: Synthetic lashes are attached to or clamped around natural lashes, adding visible length and volume without changing the natural lash.
quick.risks: Adhesives used for glued lashes can cause skin sensitivity in some people, and magnetic lashes may pose a hazard near MRI machines.
